name: Ephedrine/caffeine (ECA stack)
lead: The ECA stack is a combination of ephedrine, caffeine and aspirin used as a fat-loss and energy aid, particularly in bodybuilding and physique-cutting circles. People take it while dieting to lean out: the goal is lower body fat, which makes muscle definition, jawline and facial contours more visible, together with the appetite suppression and energy that make a calorie deficit easier to sustain.[1][2] Ephedrine is a sympathomimetic stimulant that works by prompting the release of norepinephrine, and caffeine has been described as acting synergistically with it, which is why combination products appeared.[1]

A 2021 systematic review summarized on Wikipedia reported that ephedrine, with or without caffeine, taken for roughly 4 to 24 weeks was associated with about 2 kg more weight loss than placebo.[1] A separate U.S. government-commissioned meta-analysis described modest short-term weight loss, with too little data on long-term loss or on athletic performance.[3] Ephedrine is also associated with insomnia, anxiety, raised blood pressure and fast heart rate, and in serious cases with stroke and heart attack.[1][3]

In the United States the FDA banned ephedrine-alkaloid dietary supplements in 2004 and a federal appeals court upheld the rule in 2006.[1][3] Users on looksmax.org have written ECA guides framing it as a cutting aid to be paired with exercise, and caution against it for people with heart problems.[4] Forum members on T Nation recall ephedrine-based cutting supplements as the products they considered effective before the ban.[5]

chain: Easier calorie deficit and more training energy
Sharper muscle definition and facial contours
angle.text: People use ECA while cutting to lower body fat. Less fat makes the jaw, cheekbones and musculature stand out more. The stack is described as supporting appetite control and training energy during a diet rather than changing facial structure directly.

infobox: Ephedrine-alkaloid supplements banned by FDA (2004, upheld 2006)[1][3]

paras: ECA stands for ephedrine, caffeine and aspirin. Community guides describe it as a stack for raising metabolism, suppressing appetite and boosting energy during dieting.[4] Wikipedia describes the stack as popular among bodybuilders who aim to reduce body fat before competitions.[1] On T Nation, members have also mentioned adding ephedrine and aspirin to a caffeine-containing routine for leaning out.[6]

Ephedrine induces release of norepinephrine, which indirectly activates alpha- and beta-adrenergic receptors. It also slows gastric emptying, and thermogenesis is thought to occur mainly in skeletal muscle in adults, since adults have little brown fat.[1] Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors and is widely used as an ergogenic aid; meta-analyses report improved endurance performance, and randomized trials report improved muscular endurance, strength and power with caffeine.[7][8][9]

Ephedrine alone is described as producing modest short-term weight loss, mainly fat, with unknown long-term effects. Caffeine and other methylxanthines have been reported to act synergistically with ephedrine.[1] A 2021 systematic review reported around 2 kg more weight loss than placebo over 4 to 24 weeks.[1] Wikipedia's article on ephedra cites a 6-month randomized trial of herbal ephedra and caffeine and describes the extra loss as roughly 0.9 kg per month versus placebo; whether the loss was maintained was not tested.[3]

A review commissioned by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services found modest short-term weight loss and insufficient data on performance enhancement, even though athletes widely use ephedrine.[3]

Reported effects of ephedrine include insomnia, anxiety, headache, hallucinations, high blood pressure, fast heart rate, reduced appetite and urinary retention. Stroke and heart attack have been reported as serious events.[1] By 2004 the FDA had received more than 18,000 adverse-event reports linked to ephedrine products.[1] A 2000 New England Journal of Medicine review described sudden cardiac deaths and severe disability, many in young adults using labeled doses, and a 2003 Annals of Internal Medicine study reported ephedrine alkaloids were far more likely than kava or ginkgo to cause a significant adverse reaction.[3]

Caffeine has its own documented effects on sleep. A 2023 meta-analysis of 24 studies found caffeine reduced total sleep time by about 45 minutes and sleep efficiency by 7 percent, and a 2017 review reported reduced slow-wave sleep.[10][11] A T Nation member recalled being unable to sleep until about 2 a.m. after taking ephedrine in the evening.[12] The looksmax.org guide states that the stack should not be used by people with heart problems.[4]

Ephedra (ma huang) has been documented in Chinese medicine since the Han dynasty. Ephedrine was first synthesized in 1885 by Nagai Nagayoshi, and Merck marketed it in the 1920s.[1] The FDA proposed dose limits in 1997 and withdrew parts of the proposal in 2000 after industry opposition.[3] After the death of Baltimore Orioles pitcher Steve Bechler on February 17, 2003, in which the medical examiner said ephedra toxicity played a significant role, the FDA announced action in December 2003 and issued a final rule banning ephedrine-alkaloid supplements on April 12, 2004.[3] A Utah federal judge overturned the ban in April 2005, the Tenth Circuit upheld it on August 17, 2006, and the Supreme Court declined review in May 2007.[3]

Health Canada issued a voluntary recall in January 2002 of products above 8 mg per dose, those combined with other stimulants such as caffeine, and those marketed for weight loss or bodybuilding.[1] Ephedrine is banned by several sports bodies including the NCAA, MLB, NFL and PGA.[1] Availability varies by country.[4] Ephedra extract without ephedrine alkaloids remains legally sold in the US.[3]

The Wikipedia summary cites a 2021 systematic review of ephedrine, with or without caffeine, reporting about 2 kg additional weight loss versus placebo over 4 to 24 weeks.[1] A 6-month randomized trial of herbal ephedra with caffeine (Boozer et al., 2002) is cited for modest weight loss versus placebo, and a RAND meta-analysis commissioned by the U.S. government reached similar conclusions on short-term loss.[3] No studies specific to appearance outcomes in lean, physique-focused users were found. Studies of caffeine alone cover endurance performance, strength and sleep.[7][8][9][10]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the stack is discussed in a how-to guide aimed at fat loss while cutting, and on T Nation ephedrine comes up in recollections of pre-ban cutting supplements and in physique logs.[4][5][6]

claims.claim: ECA raises metabolism and suppresses appetite for fat loss
claims.believers: The guide author describes it as a stack for metabolism, appetite suppression and energy that assists weight-loss efforts.[4] A T Nation member says cutting supplements with ephedrine were the only ones that really worked before the US ban.[5]
claims.experts: A 2021 systematic review summarized on Wikipedia found about 2 kg more weight loss than placebo over 4 to 24 weeks.[1] A government-commissioned meta-analysis found modest short-term loss and insufficient long-term data.[3]

claims.claim: It is only worthwhile alongside exercise
claims.believers: The guide says using it without exercising is pointless and compares it to taking a painkiller without pain.[4]
claims.experts: No published studies were found that test this specific claim.

claims.claim: It is safe if you have no heart problems
claims.believers: The guide warns against use with heart conditions and implies healthy users are acceptable.[4]
claims.experts: Reported effects include raised blood pressure, fast heart rate, stroke and heart attack, and sudden cardiac deaths have been described in young adults; the FDA banned ephedrine-alkaloid supplements in 2004.[1][3]

card.summary: A classic ephedrine, caffeine and aspirin cutting stack with modest reported fat-loss effects and a long regulatory history.
card.note: Ephedrine-alkaloid supplements are banned in the US; cardiovascular events have been reported.

quick.overview:
ECA combines ephedrine, caffeine and aspirin. It is used in bodybuilding and physique communities as a cutting aid for appetite suppression and energy.

A 2021 systematic review summarized on Wikipedia reported about 2 kg more weight loss than placebo over 4 to 24 weeks.
quick.mechanism: Ephedrine is a sympathomimetic stimulant; caffeine has been reported to act synergistically with it.
quick.risks: Reported effects include insomnia, anxiety, high blood pressure, fast heart rate, stroke and heart attack. The FDA banned ephedrine-alkaloid supplements in 2004; legal status varies elsewhere.
